events.text:
🇮🇱 Israel expands air defense footprint in North Africa with Morocco deal
The two countries are holding "advanced talks" about integrating Israeli David's Sling system into Morocco's air defense architecture, ES&T reports.
The system is designed to intercept ballistic missiles and cruise missiles at ranges of 40 to 300 kilometers. Each interceptor missile costs around $1 million.
Morocco already uses various Israeli-made weapon systems, including:
🔴 Barak MX and Spyder air defense systems
🔴 PULS rocket launchers
🔴 ATMOS howitzers
The deal is part of expanding military-technical cooperation between [Morocco and Israel](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75897) following the normalization of relations under the Abraham Accords. Previously, only Finland had signed deal for the supply of this system. 
The sale of the system, developed with US participation, will require American approval. However, given the deep integration of American systems into Morocco's defensive architecture, particularly Patriot systems and the expected delivery of F-16 Block 72 fighters, this is unlikely to pose an obstacle.
Notably, Algeria, Morocco's main rival on the continent, has been closely cooperating on military-technical matters with Russia, which had the opportunity to study the David's Sling's combat use in Syria.
👍 [Substack](https://geopoliticsprime.substack.com/) | [Chat](https://t.me/+HLrnOk92f31mYzIy) |

Saudi airports and airspace could face further strikes, following Saturday's deadly attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, amid an ongoing Saudi air campaign against the group, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree stated.
Saree urged the public to "take our warning seriously" and said Saudi Arabia would bear responsibility for any failed missile interceptions. The warning follows a major escalation in Saudi military operations, with the Saudi-led coalition reporting 82 airstrikes against Houthi positions across four Yemeni governorates — Saada, Al Hudaydah, Al Jawf, and Ma'rib.

events.text:
🪖 US Army's AI warfare ambitions crumble in desert training 
As rumors speculate about a potential resumption of US-Iran hostilities, a recent WSJ report depicts hard-hitting results from the latest major US military training meant to demonstrate its battle readiness.
The US Army staged a major exercise at Fort Irwin in July to demonstrate what it calls an AI-enabled battlefield, bringing 9,700 soldiers to the Mojave Desert for a mock fight against a unit standing in for China's army.
However, some of the equipment meant to represent the future of warfare failed when it mattered most.
➡️ Drones from Anduril and Theiss UAV Solutions either landed because of overheating or took ten minutes to get airborne, while spending only half their maximum flight time in the air to conserve battery
➡️ Wind gusts threw drones off course, and signals were lost behind the mountains
➡️ The augmented-reality headsets, on which three companies hold contracts worth more than $100 million each, showed deficiencies, and the army is uncertain whether it will move forward with them
As a result, the exercises mostly boiled down to training soldiers to clear buildings — a picture of outdated warfare and hardly what the American command expected to see.
The structural problems run deep
🔴 Congressional probes and government oversight reports have found the army [wasted billions](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/70744) on fumbled weapons programs, inadequate training, and failures in cybersecurity[.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/70744) New tech from startups, most of which has never been tested in war, has proven too fragile for real-world conditions
🔴 Ousted Army Secretary[ Dan Driscoll ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73962)described the current US Army as a "calcified bureaucracy," where the military cannot keep up with the pace of technological development
The last major transformation inside the Pentagon came in the 1980s, when the service pivoted from Vietnam and built the force it would use in the Gulf War. If the US military struggles to implement the newest technologies in ideal test conditions, what happens when it faces an adversary that has already mastered mass drone warfare? Iran offers a preview. Over the past year, Iranian drone and missile strikes have successfully targeted US bases across the Middle East — in Jordan, Kuwait, Bahrain, Iraq, and the UAE — forcing the Pentagon to [withdraw forces from several of them. ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75357)

🪖 Ukraine's aircraft are becoming casualties of its own arsenal
Several military jets were lost because of outdated weapons they carry, Ukrainian side says.
Due to a severe shortage of ammunition, including modern air-to-air missiles, the Ukraine is forced to use Soviet-era R-60 missiles, which are 30 to 50 years old. 
This has led to a growing number of cases in which they malfunction and explode, destroying the aircraft.
At the same time, the Ukrainian military acknowledges that it has no alternative — the R-60s are the only air-to-air missiles available in sufficient quantities.
